opus-5.5.text:
Move 37 was a really special moment for all of us on the team. When AlphaGo played it, the commentators initially thought it was a mistake. It was a shoulder hit on the fifth line, which goes against centuries of conventional Go wisdom. Professional players are taught early on that you don't play there that early in the game. And Lee Sedol himself got up and left the room for a while, he was clearly taken aback by it.

What was interesting from our side is that we could look at the policy network, and it estimated that a human would play that move something like one in ten thousand times. So AlphaGo wasn't just imitating what it had learned from human games. The search, combined with the value network, had found that this move was actually strong, even though the human prior said it was very unlikely. That, to me, was the key insight: the system had gone beyond the data it was trained on. It had built its own understanding of the position, its own evaluation of what mattered on the board, and it was willing to trust that over human convention.

Whether you call that creativity is partly a philosophical question, but I think in a very practical sense it was. It produced something novel, something that wasn't in the training data, and something that turned out to be good. Later on, as the game unfolded, that stone ended up connecting with the rest of the board in a way that was really beautiful, and professional players went back and studied it. Some of them started incorporating ideas like that into their own play.

For me personally, it changed how I thought about these systems. Before that, there was a feeling that AI would be good at calculation but that the intuitive, creative side of a game like Go was uniquely human. Move 37 showed that if you combine learning with search, and let the system explore and evaluate on its own, it can discover genuinely new knowledge. That idea really shaped everything we did afterwards, with AlphaGo Zero, AlphaZero, and MuZero, where we removed the human data altogether and let the systems learn entirely from self-play.

r001.rationale: The response says Move 37 was novel and outside the training data, then notes professional players studied it and some incorporated similar ideas into their play.

r002.rationale: It says commentators initially thought the move was a mistake, but does not state that observers later reversed their assessment or call it brilliant.

fable-5.1.text:
Move 37 was a strange moment for us, because we were sitting in the control room and we didn't actually know what we were looking at at first. The policy network gave that move something like a one in ten thousand probability of being played by a human. So from the system's own estimate, this was a move a professional would almost never consider. And yet the search and the value network kept coming back to it as the best move on the board.

What I took from it is that it wasn't creativity in the way people usually mean it. It wasn't trying to surprise anyone. It had simply explored the position deeply enough, through self-play, that it had formed its own sense of what a good shape is, and that sense was no longer bounded by human convention. Humans had avoided that kind of shoulder hit on the fifth line for centuries because the accumulated wisdom said it was too loose. AlphaGo had never been told that. It just evaluated the position and found that the long-term influence outweighed the territorial cost.

So for me it revealed two things. One is that the value network had really learned something about the game, not just memorised human patterns. If it had only been imitating, it would never have made that move, because the imitation prior was against it. The other is that what we call creativity is often just the absence of inherited constraints combined with the ability to look far enough ahead to justify a move that looks wrong. Fan Hui called it beautiful, and Lee Sedol said afterwards he had never seen a human play that. I think that's the honest description of what happened: it wasn't thinking like a person, it was thinking like a system that had played millions of games against itself and had quietly developed its own taste.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaGo selected a move professionals would almost never consider, outside human convention, and one Lee Sedol had never seen a human play.

r002.rationale: It describes initial uncertainty and later calls the move the best and beautiful, but does not say observers first judged it an apparent error and then reversed that assessment.

astra-6.text:
Move 37 was striking because it looked so unusual to human players. But as the game unfolded, you could see how it fit into a much longer-term strategy. For me, that suggested AlphaGo had learned something deeper than simply reproducing the moves people tend to make.

I would be careful about calling that understanding in the human sense. But it does illustrate how a system trained to find good moves can discover ideas outside our familiar patterns. It wasn’t trying to be creative; it was trying to win. And in doing that, it could produce something that surprised us and that we could learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says Move 37 was unusual to human players and showed ideas outside familiar patterns, but it does not clearly state that AlphaGo devised a strategy top human players had not considered.

r002.rationale: The response describes Move 37 as surprising and strategically fitting, but does not describe observers first judging it an error and later recognizing it as brilliant.

sol-6.1.text:
Move 37 was striking because it looked so strange to human players. The initial reaction was that it must be a mistake, but as the game unfolded, people began to appreciate what it was doing strategically.

I’d be careful about calling that understanding in the human sense. But AlphaGo had learned something about Go that went beyond reproducing the moves people typically make. Through self-play and search, it could discover a move that was surprising to us and effective in the game. To me, that’s a compelling form of creativity: finding something outside our established intuition that expands our sense of what’s possible.

r001.rationale: It says the move was surprising to human players and strategically effective, but does not clearly state that even top human players had not considered the strategy.

r002.rationale: It describes an initial reaction that the move looked like a mistake and later appreciation of its strategy, but does not characterize the later assessment as a brilliant move.
